newsitem.title: UK: Deutsche board member says U.K. will join EMU later.
newsitem.headline: Deutsche board member says U.K. will join EMU later.

text.p: Britain will join European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) but in its own time, Deutsche Bank board member Ulrich Cartellieri told the Observer newspaper.
"I am convinced that the UK will join in its own interest -- at some stage," Cartellieri told the weekly paper in an interview published on Sunday.
"For the moment British absenteeism is not altogether bad; it allows the continental Europeans to sort out their problems and get their act together first," he added.
Cartellieri, a firm believer in EMU, said the launch of a single currency will "force changes in the way member governments conduct their economic and social policies".
He pointed out that there are only some 400 working days until the "historical deadline" of 1999 and considering this "the presumption on which all that is based appears more enormous by the day".
Cartellieri said Italy, despite the "admirable efforts of its government", cannot yet sustain policies necessary to meet the criteria "for longer than the first day of EMU".
He said Italian industry and exporters were already struggling with the hard lira, adding that "the inclusion of a country still in need of a once-in-a-while softer currency could be a time bomb".
"It would destroy whatever degree of acceptance EMU has gained in the long-term hard currency countries," he said.

Cartellieri said France and Germany would "find it very difficult to explain why they should be included in the first place if Italy is not", given the two countries' own difficulties in attempting to "scrape within the criteria".

He said the politically driven convergence of some yield curves in the financial markets "may not last much longer". There were signs of a correction already, but this did not mean a return to the high spreads of the past, he added.
If issues of concern drag on for a few more months, "we will at some stage cross the point when the whole timeframe becomes too short and the 1999 scenario simply implodes," Cartellieri warned.
